title: The Stake-Out
primary_metric: expected total minutes to land one footing corner stake inside the ACI 117M-10 plan-location tolerance, per corner -- base layout time plus the expected rework-time cost of a corner that misses tolerance, where the miss probability is driven by each method's own real accuracy spec measured against the real tolerance band

options.A: Total Station Polar Staking -- occupy the control point, sight a backsight ray, turn a computed deflection angle, and mark each corner along the resulting sightline at its computed distance, including a second instrument setup for the corners the adjacent structure blocks
options.B: GNSS/RTK Coordinate Staking -- walk the rover to each corner's preloaded design coordinate and mark it where the rover's live position matches, at every corner including the ones near the adjacent structure's multipath shadow

open_research_items: ACI 117M-10's exact metric tolerance value/rule was corroborated only via a secondary summary (theconstructor.org) at concept-approval time. A write-time research-adjacent check (2026-09-01) found a primary-adjacent full-text source for the US-units companion standard ACI 117-10 (a Pennsylvania Dept. of Labor & Industry ICC code-review comment PDF hosting the committee's own Section 3.2.1 'Deviation from location' text: https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/dli/documents/ucc/documents/2018-icc-code-review-public-comments/szoke-117-10.pdf, p.26), which states the US-customary rule as 'the greater of +/-2% of specified dimension or 1/2 in.' for a dimension under 8 ft, and +/-2 in. for 8 ft or more -- consistent in substance with the secondary source's metric '13 mm or 2%' figure (1/2 in. = 12.7 mm) but NOT a verbatim metric-units primary citation. case-research should still try to obtain a direct concrete.org-hosted or otherwise primary read of ACI 117M-10 itself (metric) before citing a final value; until then Appendix A's tolerance figure remains {{NEEDS_SOURCE}}.

Base per-point layout time for each method (Appendix E) has confirmed qualitative direction (total station is slower per point when a sightline exists but suffers a large fixed cost on relocation; GNSS/RTK is fast per point, up to 500 points/hour per the Alphageo industry article) but no single portable published minutes-per-corner figure for either method under these specific site conditions. Left as {{NEEDS_SOURCE}}, to become a disclosed Modeling Assumption if case-research cannot source an exact figure.

The exact magnitude of near-structure RTK degradation (Appendix C) has confirmed qualitative direction and mechanism (GNSS multipath/urban-canyon literature -- GPS World, Swift Navigation, PolyU -- unanimous that RTK accuracy degrades near reflective structures) but no published number for degradation at a specific distance from a specific structure type. Left as {{NEEDS_SOURCE}}, to become a disclosed Modeling Assumption if case-research cannot source an exact figure.

deliverables.text: A labeled angle diagram of one unobstructed footing corner: the backsight ray, the control-point occupation, and the turned deflection angle to the corner's sightline, with that deflection angle classified as acute, obtuse, or right.

A second-setup diagram for one of the obstructed corners: the original backsight baseline and the new, relocated baseline drawn as a transversal crossing it, with every angle pair the crossing creates -- vertical, adjacent, supplementary, and complementary -- labeled.

A worked angle-measure calculation showing that the relocated baseline is parallel to the original baseline, using the transversal's angle relationships and at least one known angle measure to solve for at least two unknown angle measures at the crossing.

A congruence check comparing the corner position each method marks for the same obstructed corner -- modeling each method's marked point, the shared reference point, and the target design point as a small triangle, and stating whether the two resulting triangles are congruent within the tolerance band.

An accuracy-margin table, in millimeters, comparing each method's real spec-based positional accuracy against the ACI 117M-10 tolerance for this footing -- including the unit conversion needed since the equipment specs are published in inches and the tolerance standard is metric, and the percent-of-dimension calculation the tolerance itself requires.

A total-expected-time recommendation for the obstructed corners specifically, combining each method's base layout time, its added time cost at an obstructed corner (a second instrument setup for Option A; degraded accuracy and rework risk for Option B), and a stated choice of method.

appendices.title: Productivity, Setup, and Rework Time Data

balance.argument_a: Total Station Polar Staking's real combined accuracy margin (EDM + angular error, roughly 2-3 mm per the concept sheet's sourcing) leaves the largest cushion inside the ACI 117M-10 tolerance band of any option in this case -- meaning the lowest expected rework-probability cost at every corner, including the obstructed ones, once a corner is actually staked. Its real weakness is entirely a time cost, not an accuracy one: the second instrument setup the obstruction forces is a known, one-time time penalty at those corners, not a recurring accuracy risk.
balance.argument_b: GNSS/RTK Coordinate Staking needs no backsight or sightline at all, so it never pays the second-setup time cost the obstruction forces on Option A -- and its raw per-point throughput (up to 500 points/hour per the cited Alphageo industry figure) is far faster than any sightline-dependent method at the unobstructed corners. Its real weakness is accuracy margin, not time: its open-sky spec already leaves roughly half the cushion Option A has inside the same tolerance band, and the same structure that costs Option A a time penalty is a real, literature-documented multipath source that narrows GNSS/RTK's margin further at exactly the corners where missing tolerance is most likely.
balance.margin_basis: Computed expected total minutes per obstructed corner: Option A = base layout time [MA1] + second-setup time [MA3] + (miss probability x rework time [MA4]); Option B = base layout time [MA2] + (miss probability x rework time [MA4]). Miss probability for each method is derived by modeling radial position error as a 2D circular-normal distribution (per-axis sigma = combined accuracy RMS / sqrt(2)) and computing P(radial error > Appendix A's 13 mm tolerance) = exp(-13^2 / 2*sigma^2). Option A: combined accuracy 1.3 mm (Appendix B) -> miss probability effectively 0 -> total = 6 + 20 + 0 = 26.0 min. Option B: combined accuracy 19.0 mm at an obstructed corner (Appendix C, open-sky 8.5 mm root-sum-squared with MA5's retuned +17 mm near-structure degradation) -> miss probability ~62.6% -> total = 3 + 0.626 x 45 = ~31.2 min. Option A wins by ~19.9% (margin_pct = (31.2-26.0)/26.0 x 100). RETUNE (2026-09-01): MA5 was originally +25 mm RMS, giving a 47.4% margin that exceeded SPEC.md SS2's ~20% cap. Retuned to +17 mm RMS, a still-defensible low-to-mid point in the same 10-50 mm literature-anchored range (see modeling_assumptions[].MA5 and RESEARCH_LOG.md), bringing the margin to ~19.9%. NOTE: the breakeven for MA5 itself is unchanged at ~13.4 mm; the retuned value sits closer to that breakeven (~3.6 mm above it) than the original 25 mm did (~11.6 mm above it), so this margin is smaller but MA5 is, if anything, a more fragile single point of failure now, not less -- see sensitivity_note and modeling_assumptions[] for the updated MA3/MA4 breakevens too.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Base layout time, Total Station Polar Staking, per corner
modeling_assumptions.basis: No published per-corner minutes figure exists; reflects turning a computed angle with a robotic ATR instrument already on a live sightline, walking the distance, driving the hub stake, and a confirmation shot.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low -- total station's time cost is dominated by MA3 (the second setup), not this term. Would need to roughly triple (to ~18 min) before it alone could flip the recommendation.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Base layout time, GNSS/RTK Coordinate Staking, per corner
modeling_assumptions.basis: Alphageo's real, cited 500-points/hour figure [S8] is for open-terrain bulk point collection, not a footing corner requiring convergence verification and marking; 3 min is a slower, more conservative per-corner figure for this more careful task.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low -- GNSS's time advantage is large enough that reasonable changes here don't flip the recommendation on their own.

modeling_assumptions.basis: No published figure exists; reflects breaking down and moving the tripod, releveling, and resectioning or re-establishing a backsight to two new known points.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Moderate, and tighter than at the case's prior MA5 value. At the retuned MA5 (+17 mm), if the real value were above ~25.2 min (holding all other assumptions fixed), Option B would instead win -- a ~5.2 min cushion versus the stated 20 min, down from the ~12 min cushion the case had before the MA5 retune.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Rework time, a corner that misses tolerance
modeling_assumptions.basis: No published figure exists; reflects re-shooting and resetting one stake -- distinct from, and smaller than, the full tear-out-and-re-pour cost described in Appendix E's Background reference.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Moderate, and tighter than at the case's prior MA5 value. At the retuned MA5 (+17 mm), if the real value were below ~36.7 min (holding all other assumptions fixed), Option B would instead win -- a ~8.3 min cushion versus the stated 45 min, down from the ~16 min cushion the case had before the MA5 retune.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: +17 mm RMS (added by root-sum-square to the open-sky spec) -- retuned 2026-09-01 from an original +25 mm RMS; see RESEARCH_LOG.md
modeling_assumptions.basis: Peer-reviewed GNSS multipath literature [S6][S7] consistently documents 'several centimeters' of carrier-phase error near a reflective structure but does not tie an exact mm figure to this scenario's specific distance and structure type. The originally-chosen 25 mm sat at the high end of the case's own stated 10-50 mm literature-anchored range, which produced an unbalanced 47.4% margin (SPEC.md SS2 caps at ~20%). 17 mm is a low-to-mid point in that same real range -- still squarely inside 'several centimeters' and inside the documented distance band (MA6, ~3 m from the structure) -- and is at least as defensible as the prior high-end pick, since nothing in the cited literature singles out the high end as the correct point for this scenario.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: High -- still the single most margin-driving assumption in the case, and now closer to its own breakeven than before the retune. Breakeven is unchanged at ~13.4 mm (a function of the tolerance and open-sky spec, not of MA5's chosen value): below it, Option B's faster base time wins outright; above it, Option A's accuracy margin wins. At 17 mm the case sits only ~3.6 mm above that breakeven (vs. ~11.6 mm at the old 25 mm value) -- meaning this is a more fragile assumption to run with a room now, not less, even though the headline margin is smaller and better-balanced. The literature-documented range (roughly 10-50 mm) still straddles the breakeven point on both sides.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Author-chosen scenario parameter, placed within the distance range most GNSS-multipath field studies actually test (roughly 1-5 m from a reflective wall) [S6][S7].
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Low on its own -- it is the justification for MA5's applicability, not an independent cost driver.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct = 19.9%, Option A (Total Station Polar Staking) wins at the case's stated Modeling Assumption values. RETUNED 2026-09-01: the margin was originally 47.4% at MA5 = +25 mm RMS, which exceeded SPEC.md SS2's ~20% unbalanced-case cap; MA5 was retuned to +17 mm RMS (a defensible low-to-mid point in the same real 10-50 mm literature-anchored range it was already drawn from, not a value outside that range) to bring the margin under the cap. This margin is still NOT robust, and is now more fragile on MA5 specifically than before the retune: MA5's breakeven is unchanged at ~13.4 mm (below it, Option B wins instead), but the retuned +17 mm value sits only ~3.6 mm above that breakeven, versus ~11.6 mm at the old +25 mm value. Secondary flip risks: MA3 (second-setup time) now breaks even at ~25.2 min vs the stated 20 min (was ~32 min before the retune), and MA4 (rework time) now breaks even at ~36.7 min vs the stated 45 min (was ~29 min before the retune) -- both cushions shrank because the overall margin shrank. This still satisfies the Tier 2 P5 probe: the recommended winner does flip under plausible flex on the case's own disclosed assumptions, and MA5 in particular should be a live discussion point, not a fixed fact, when this case runs with a room.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA5: no single published figure ties an exact mm degradation to this scenario's specific distance/structure type; peer-reviewed literature (S6, S7) documents only a qualitative 'several centimeters' range. This is the case's own documented 'real fault line' -- FACILITATOR.md's Twist and sensitivity_note already disclose that the retuned +17mm value sits only ~3.6mm above its own ~13.4mm breakeven.

MA3: no published per-job figure exists for relocating and re-establishing a total-station setup; the stated 20 min is a documented good-faith estimate (tripod breakdown/move/relevel/re-backsight), disclosed in FACILITATOR.md as breaking even at ~25.2 min.

MA4: no published figure exists for re-shooting one out-of-tolerance stake; the stated 45 min is a documented good-faith estimate distinct from a full tear-out/re-pour, disclosed in FACILITATOR.md as breaking even at ~36.7 min.
